A content delivery network solves a simple problem: the internet has distance, and distance creates delay. Every website lives somewhere specific — that home base is called the origin server, the single computer (or cluster) storing the real, original files. If everyone visiting a website had to fetch data from that one origin, no matter where they were on the planet, pages would load slowly for anyone far away. So a content delivery network stores copies of that content on servers scattered across many cities worldwide, called edge locations, because they sit at the "edge" of the network, close to actual visitors instead of far away at the origin. Think of it like a chain of bakeries that all sell bread baked at one central factory — instead of shipping a fresh loaf across the country for every single customer, the factory sends batches to local branches, so nearby shoppers get bread quickly without waiting for a cross-country delivery. When a visitor requests a page, the nearby edge location checks whether it already has a saved copy; finding one is called a cache hit, and it means the content can be delivered instantly, skipping the long trip to the origin entirely. Only when nothing suitable is stored nearby does the request travel further. The result is faster loading, less strain on the original source, and a smoother experience regardless of location.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | Everything else is ultimately copied from here |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding a stored copy of content | Shortens the distance data has to travel |
| Cache hit | A successful find of saved content nearby | Means instant delivery, no long trip needed |
| Cache miss | Nearby copy not found, so origin gets contacted | Explains occasional slower first-time loads |
